Spiritual Formation
SPIR-it-choo-ul for-MAY-shun
n. phrase (practical and ascetical theology; the deliberate shaping of a believer's soul toward Christlikeness through the Spirit's work in the ordinary means of grace)
Spiritual from Latin spiritualis, from spiritus (breath, Spirit); relating to the Holy Spirit's work and the immaterial dimension of human life. Formation from Latin formatio — formare (to form, shape) — the act of being given a definite shape or character. In the classical theological sense, spiritual formation names what God does to the believer through the Spirit by means of Word, prayer, and sacrament: He forms Christ in them (Gal 4:19), working the image of the Son into every dimension of the soul.

See also: Spiritual Formation

Biblical Definition

Spiritual formation — in its biblical sense — is the Spirit's work of conforming the believer progressively to the image of Christ through the ordinary means of grace: the Word preached and read, prayer, the Lord's Supper, baptism, fellowship, and suffering. The Apostle Paul names the goal: “Him we proclaim — admonishing every person and teaching every person in all wisdom — so that we may present every person mature in Christ” (Col 1:28). The means is not technique but the Spirit who uses His appointed instruments. Paul's labor-pain metaphor in Galatians 4:19 — “until Christ is formed in you” — describes the apostolic investment in the church's formation: it is agonizing, personal, patient, and directed toward a Person (Christ), not a set of spiritual competencies. Philippians 2:12–13 holds the active and passive together: “work out your salvation with fear and trembling — for it is God who is at work in you both to will and to work for His good pleasure.” The believer's effort (the means) and God's sovereign operation (the efficient cause) are not competitors but co-operating realities. Hebrews 12:14 adds the ecclesial horizon: “pursue the sanctification without which no one will see the Lord.” Spiritual formation in the Reformed sense is therefore always Word-and-Spirit driven, means-of-grace-centered, and directed toward visible holiness within the covenant community — never private mysticism or self-designed technique.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Spirit's progressive work of conforming the believer to the image of Christ through the ordinary means of grace — Word, prayer, sacrament, and suffering — as distinct from self-designed spiritual technique or contemplative mysticism borrowed from Catholic ascetical tradition.

SPIRITUAL FORMATION, n. phrase. The process by which a believer is shaped into the likeness of Christ through the Holy Spirit's work in and through the ordinary means of grace. The biblical language is “formed” (Gal 4:19, morphoo — given the definitive shape of Christ within the soul), “conformed” (Rom 8:29, summorphos — bearing together the same form as), and “transformed” (Rom 12:2, metamorphoo — the ongoing renewal of the mind). All three Greek terms point to the Spirit's active shaping work, not to techniques the believer masters.

The Reformed tradition grounds spiritual formation in the means of grace, not in spiritual exercises developed apart from them. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 154) names the outward means: the Word (read, preached, and heard), the sacraments, and prayer — these are the ordinary channels through which the Spirit works. The extraordinary and the self-designed are suspect; the ordinary and the appointed are sufficient.

The Puritan tradition produced the richest practical literature of Reformed spiritual formation: John Owen's On the Mortification of Sin (1656), Thomas Watson's A Body of Practical Divinity (1692), and Richard Baxter's The Saints' Everlasting Rest (1650) expose the inner life, name the Spirit's instruments, and resist any shortcut that bypasses the Word. This is the model — not the contemplative exercises of Ignatius Loyola or the centering-prayer tradition of Thomas Merton.

Galatians 4:19 gives the goal and the agent: Paul travails in birth pains “until Christ is formed in you.” The goal is not spiritual wellness, emotional health, or a generic flourishing; it is Christ — the Person, the character, the obedience — reproduced in every dimension of the believer's life by the Spirit through the Word.

Philippians 2:12–13 supplies the pattern for the believer's active role: “work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you.” The divine sovereignty does not produce passivity; it produces strenuous, humble, reverent activity directed at holiness — which is exactly what the Puritan tradition called “practical religion.”

Key Scripture

Colossians 1:28 — "Him we proclaim — admonishing every person and teaching every person in all wisdom — so that we may present every person mature in Christ."

Galatians 4:19 — "My children, with whom I am again in labor pains until Christ is formed in you —"

Philippians 2:12 — "Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed — not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence — work out your salvation with fear and trembling."

Hebrews 12:14 — "Pursue peace with all men — and the sanctification without which no one will see the Lord."

Modern Corruption

The modern “spiritual formation movement” — driven by Richard Foster's Celebration of Discipline and Dallas Willard's works — has imported Catholic contemplative practices (centering prayer, lectio divina as mystical technique, solitude exercises) into evangelical churches in place of the Word-and-Spirit ordinary means of grace.

expand to see more

Richard Foster's Celebration of Discipline (1978) became the generative text of the modern spiritual formation movement in evangelicalism and drew heavily on medieval Catholic mysticism — Thomas à Kempis, Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross, and Thomas Merton — to construct a set of “spiritual disciplines” presented as the universal Christian path to formation. Dallas Willard's The Spirit of the Disciplines (1988) and Renovation of the Heart (2002) gave the movement its theoretical architecture. While both authors contain useful material on practice and intentionality, the movement as a whole has tended to substitute contemplative technique — particularly “centering prayer,” a practice derived from Basil Pennington's reading of Merton and the Desert Fathers — for the means of grace appointed by Christ in Scripture. Centering prayer's method of emptying the mind of all content to receive God's presence is incompatible with biblical prayer, which is addressed, specific, and saturated with the Word.

The deeper problem of the spiritual formation movement is methodological: it treats formation as something the believer achieves through selected practices rather than something the Spirit works through appointed means. This is not the Reformed distinction between means and end; it is a subtle synergism of technique. The Reformers and Puritans were not opposed to discipline — they were the most disciplined practitioners of Word-saturated daily life in Christian history — but they located the formative power in the Word preached and the Spirit who uses it, not in techniques borrowed from sources the Reformers deliberately corrected. Reformation-and-beyond spiritual formation is: preach the Word, pray the Psalms, take the Lord's Supper, mortify the flesh, and wait on the God who forms His people through His own appointed means.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Spiritual formation in the biblical sense is rooted in the Pauline formation language (Gal 4:19; Rom 8:29; 12:2), the Westminster means-of-grace theology, the Puritan practical divinity tradition, and the 1689 LBCF's account of the Spirit's work in sanctification.

expand to see more

Galatians 4:19 / Romans 8:29 / Romans 12:2 — the three Pauline formation terms (morphoo, summorphos, metamorphoo); all three locate the formative agency in God's Spirit shaping the believer into the image of the Son, not in the believer's technique.

Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 154–158 — the appointed means of grace (Word, sacraments, prayer) as the ordinary channels of the Spirit's formative work; the catechism's account is the best Reformed summary of the mechanics of spiritual formation.

John Owen, On the Mortification of Sin (1656) — the Puritan practical-formation masterwork; Owen's central axiom — “Be killing sin or it will be killing you” — epitomizes the active-yet-Spirit-dependent character of Reformed formation.

Thomas Watson, A Body of Practical Divinity (1692) / Richard Baxter, The Reformed Pastor (1656) — the corporate dimension of Reformed formation: the pastor's role in shaping the congregation through preaching, catechizing, and personal pastoral care.

1689 LBCF, Chapter 13 (Of Sanctification) — the confession's account of progressive, Spirit-wrought, Word-saturated sanctification as the Reformed framework for understanding what spiritual formation is and is not.

Usage

"When a church adopts a “spiritual formation curriculum” built around centering prayer and contemplative silence, it has replaced the Reformed means of grace with Catholic ascetical technique; the corrective is not to abandon intentionality in discipleship but to reground it in the Word preached, the Psalms prayed, and the Supper taken."

"Galatians 4:19 reveals that spiritual formation is apostolic labor, not self-improvement: Paul is in labor pains until Christ is formed in the Galatians, meaning formation is a pastoral investment that requires the Word proclaimed and applied — not a personal retreat to a monastery."

"The danger of the formation movement is not emphasis on discipline (the Puritans out-disciplined anyone) but the source of the disciplines: practices derived from Catholic mysticism carry assumptions about the nature of God's presence and the role of the mind in prayer that are incompatible with the Protestant sola Scriptura framework."
